papers.title: Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Zhiguang Yang, Yulin Yang, Fuyu Lv, Dan Ou
papers.summary: Taobao search CTR models mainly remember historical clicks through item IDs, so ==the same item with a different main image is almost indistinguishable to the model==. FineSID turns each item image into 30 discrete codes across four VAR tokenizer scales from 1×1 to 4×4, tokenizes titles and OCR text by field, and looks them all up like ordinary ID features; the shared network is first trained on query–item relevance labels from a Qwen3.5 teacher, then fine-tuned with a click head on click logs. Offline AUC is 0.25 points above the HiFormer baseline and 0.38 points higher on cold items; a seven-day Taobao main-search A/B test raised GMV by 0.85%.

deep_reading.title: Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction
deep_reading.content:
Taobao search's fine-ranking CTR models mainly remember historical clicks through user, query, and item ID features. ==The same item with a different main image or a rewritten title keeps the same item ID, so the model's score barely changes==; newly listed, rarely clicked items have learned little from the ID itself. Alibaba's FineSID splits item images and text into fine-grained discrete codes and looks them up together with ordinary ID features into the same ranking network: images become 30 position-aware codes across four VAR tokenizer scales from 1×1 to 4×4; titles and OCR text are tokenized per field. Training has two stages: first train the whole network on LLM-labeled query–item relevance, then swap in a click head and fine-tune all parameters on click logs. Offline AUC is 0.25 points above the HiFormer baseline and 0.38 points higher on cold items; a seven-day Taobao main-search A/B test shows click +0.21% and GMV +0.85%.

The overall structure has three stages: offline, turn content into discrete codes; pretrain the shared network on relevance labels; fine-tune for personalization on click labels. Stages two and three share one network and only swap the output head.

## 1. Problem: how content enters an ID model

Industrial CTR models are mainly ID embeddings plus a feature-crossing network. Multimodal content usually enters in one of three ways. First, jointly train an image encoder end to end—too expensive. Second, concatenate continuous vectors from a pretrained model, for example the LEARN-style baseline that concatenates Qwen3.5 content vectors; continuous vectors and sparse IDs have different distributions and often only fuse in late layers. Third, semantic IDs (SID): quantize a whole item's content vector into a few discrete codes and look them up like IDs—RQ-VAE SID is representative.

The authors agree with the third direction but say the granularity is too coarse. RQ-VAE compresses a whole image into a few codes and loses spatial detail such as "is there a promo badge in the top-left" or "what color is the model wearing"; two main images of the same item can get the same codes. FineSID wants to keep those details without running an image model online.

## 2. Method

### 2.1 Content → discrete codes

Images use VAR's pretrained tokenizer. VAR generates images scale by scale; its tokenizer is trained for reconstruction and encodes an image into multi-scale code maps. FineSID takes scales 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, and 4×4—1+4+9+16 = 30 codes per image. Coarse scales capture overall style; fine scales capture local regions.

Codes are computed offline and stored; online serving only adds 30 table lookups and does not run an image model. The ranking network's embedding tables for these codes are randomly initialized and trained with the task, independent of VAR's reconstruction codebook. Flattening keeps a fixed "which scale, which cell" order, so the same position always enters the same input slot.

For text, query, title, and OCR each use their own BPE and n-gram vocabularies; each field stays an independent token sequence rather than being collapsed into one summary vector.

### 2.2 Shared prediction network

The three input types meet as follows. Text fields first do cross-attention: query embeddings as queries, title and OCR token embeddings as keys/values, yielding text representations weighted by the current query. Then ordered fusion concatenates, in a fixed order, the original ID-feature embeddings, the 30 visual-code embeddings, and each field's text representation.

The long vector is projected to 768-d, then through two HiFormer layers. HiFormer is Google's feature-crossing structure; here its latent-slot attention maps inputs onto a small fixed set of slots to avoid quadratic self-attention over thousands of tokens. An MLP 768→256→64 yields a 64-d shared representation $h$ for the output head.

![FineSID framework. Left three rows are inputs: images through the VAR tokenizer into four-scale codes; text through BPE / n-gram; plus original ID features. Middle is the shared prediction network—see the Ordered fusion → Projection → HiFormer → Shared MLP column. Right top is the stage-2 relevance head; right bottom is the stage-3 click head; both stages share the entire middle column.](figs/2610.29138/fig1_framework.png)

### 2.3 Relevance first, then clicks

Stage 2 pretrains on relevance. Each impression gets a four-way soft relevance distribution from a Qwen3.5 model fine-tuned on millions of human labels; the network fits soft-label cross-entropy:

$$L_{rel}=-\mathbb{E}_x\sum_{k=1}^{4}t_k(x)\log\pi_{\theta,\psi_{rel},k}(x)$$

$t_k(x)$ is the teacher's probability for tier $k$, $\pi$ the network's prediction, $\theta$ shared-network parameters, $\psi_{rel}$ the relevance head. The intent is for SID embeddings and crossing layers to learn "does this image and title match this query" first—clicks alone learn that slowly because clicks mix price and brand preference.

Stage 3 drops the relevance head, attaches a randomly initialized click head, and fine-tunes all parameters—including SID embeddings, ID embeddings, crossing layers, and normalization stats—with binary cross-entropy on click logs. The authors stress this is full-parameter transfer, unlike migrating only embeddings and discarding upper layers.

## 3. Experiments

Data are real Taobao search impressions: seven days Aug 25–31 for training (~51.2B impressions, 251M users, 418M items); one day Sep 1 for eval (453M impressions). Metrics are AUC, query-grouped GAUC, and the same two on the cold-item subset with under 1,000 views that day. Taobao numbers are absolute differences versus the HiFormer baseline, in percentage points.

**Main results versus other content-injection methods.** This shows fine-grained codes beat whole-image vectors and coarse SIDs. Controls all add content on the same HiFormer backbone: Visual ID quantizes visual vectors into discrete IDs; COINS aligns SID content with collaborative signals for cold start; PRECTR and Joint relevance + CTR are two ways to bring relevance supervision into CTR.

FineSID leads every column; cold-subset gains exceed full-set gains, matching "content codes fill in when ID signal is scarce." LEARN-style continuous concatenation only gains +0.05 AUC; Joint relevance + CTR is below the baseline on the cold subset.

**Same-item creative discrimination.** This rules out "the model only memorized item IDs." Item ID is fixed; only creatives (main image, title) differ. Metric is NSCTR: for each impression, the model picks the highest-scoring creative among that item's candidates; a match with the logged creative counts, and matching impressions' CTR is weighted by the item's original impression count. ==Candidates share the exact same ID, so score gaps can only come from content==. FineSID's relative NSCTR gain is 0.75%; COINS is 0.27%.

![How NSCTR is computed (drawn). Several creatives of the same item differ only in content; a match between the model's top-scoring creative and the logged one contributes that item's replay CTR.](figs/2610.29138/nsctr_replay.svg)

**Ablations: what each stage contributes.**

Dropping SID nearly zeros the gain and slightly hurts cold AUC—most of the lift is the content codes themselves. Relevance pretraining adds another 0.05 AUC and matters more for NSCTR (0.51% → 0.75%). Mean pooling cuts more than half of the AUC gain, so keeping position and field identity helps.

**Public MMCTR.** MMCTR has no relevance labels, so only the version without stage 2 is tested. HiFormer baseline AUC 0.9767; FineSID reaches 0.9844 (+0.77 points), above COINS 0.9825 and LEARN-style 0.9823.

**Online A/B.** Seven days on Taobao main search versus the production model: click +0.21%, GMV +0.85%, both significant. The authors report no significant fine-rank latency increase because the 30 visual codes are extracted offline and online only adds lookups and a wider first projection.

## 4. Limitations

The authors list three: the VAR tokenizer is trained for reconstruction and frozen in stage 2, so codes are not optimized for search semantics; relevance pretraining is only shown transferring to CTR, not to retrieval or conversion; 30 codes widen the concatenated vector and need more work for million-candidate retrieval.

One more: MMCTR only tests the version without relevance pretraining, so the full three-stage pipeline has evidence from only one Taobao data source; online GMV +0.85% with click only +0.21% is not broken down by which item types drive the GMV lift.

## 5. Takeaways for fine-ranking teams

If your fine-ranker already has a content-vector feature with little gain, try FineSID's idea: replace images with multi-scale, position-aware discrete codes that share the same embedding lookup path as IDs; online cost is mainly storage and lookups.

If you already have relevance labels or a relevance model, pretrain the whole ranking network on it, then fully fine-tune on clicks. In the ablation this step helps same-item creative discrimination (NSCTR) the most—useful when you need multi-image, multi-title creative selection.

papers.title: Generative Recommenders Forget the Long Tail: Restoring Memorization in Retrieval and Ranking
papers.authors: Xu Huang, Jiancan Wu, Hongzheng Qin, Jiawei Feng, Can Ye, Wencong Zeng, Fengze Li, Xiang Wang
papers.summary: Generative recommenders use beam search to emit item-ID tokens one by one, and ==tail items have low generation probability and are often pruned in the first one or two steps==: on Amazon Industrial & Scientific, MiniOneRec's 50 candidates cover only 11.94% of tail targets. CAPE does not retrain the model; at inference it counts which items co-occurred with the user's history in the training data, retrieves 25 extra tail candidates by that count, and adds the count into the ranking score. On LastFM, TIGER's top-10 hit rate on tail targets rises from 3.94% to 17.19%, with 11–16% extra latency per request.

deep_reading.title: Generative Recommenders Forget the Long Tail: Restoring Memorization in Retrieval and Ranking
deep_reading.content:
Generative recommenders encode each item as a short token ID, generate those tokens from the user history one by one, keep only the 50 highest-probability partial sequences at each step, and finally rank candidates by the same generation probability. ==Tail items have low probability and are often dropped in the first one or two steps==: on Amazon Industrial & Scientific, MiniOneRec's 50 candidates cover only 11.94% of tail targets in the test set; when the authors inject 25 extra tail candidates per user—135 new tail targets in total—none of them enter the top 10 under generation-probability ranking. CAPE does not retrain the model; at inference it counts from the training data which items co-occurred with the user history under the same users, retrieves 25 extra tail candidates with that count, and adds the count into the ranking score. On LastFM, TIGER's top-10 hit rate on tail targets rises from 3.94% to 17.19%; across the paper's experiments, per-request latency rises only 11–16%.

## 1. Setting the scene

Generative recommendation has been hot in industry, led by models such as TIGER and OneRec. Unlike dual-tower retrieval, it builds no vector index. Each item is first encoded as a short ID—say three tokens—called a semantic ID (SID); items with similar content or representation share the same first few tokens. At serving time the model reads the user history, generates the first token, then the second and third, and a complete ID is one candidate item.

Users need more than one candidate, so generation uses beam search: at each step only the B highest-probability sequences so far are kept and the rest are dropped. This paper sets B to 50 and ends with 50 candidates. Ranking uses no second model; candidates are sorted by the probability of generating that item ID and the top 10 are shown. Recall and ranking share one score.

The paper focuses on tail items, defined as the bottom 80% by training-set frequency—called the long tail below. They make up more than half of test targets: 57.8% on Amazon Industrial & Scientific (I&S below), 51.1% on Amazon Office Products (Office), and 64.2% on LastFM.

## 2. Why the long tail is pruned at retrieval

Beam search compares probabilities of partially generated prefixes. The paper proves an intuitive fact with the chain rule: a prefix's probability equals the sum of probabilities of all items that start with it (Proposition 2.2).

$$p_\theta(z_{\le t}\mid H_u)=\sum_{c:\,z_{\le t}(c)=z_{\le t}} p_\theta(c\mid H_u)+\epsilon_\theta(z_{\le t}).$$

$z_{\le t}$ is the first $t$ tokens of an ID, $H_u$ the user history, $c$ an item, and $\epsilon$ the probability of generating a nonexistent ID (zero when normalizing only over legal tokens).

So whether a prefix survives depends on the summed probability of all items under it, not on the best single item. Maximum-likelihood training already assigns low probability to tail items, so their prefixes often fail to stay in the top 50 at the first step.

Can one simply boost prefixes of tail items? The authors check and find that 99.97%, 96.21%, and 99.95% of tail items on I&S, Office, and LastFM share their first token with at least one head item. ==Boosting that prefix also boosts the head items under the same prefix==.

Ranking cannot recover what was lost. As long as the top 10 are chosen from 50 candidates, the best possible tail hit rate is the share of tail targets that landed in the candidate set. Anything dropped at retrieval cannot be recovered by any later reranker (Proposition 2.1).

![Top-left: with the same four items, the head-item prefix sums to probability 0.10 while the tail target t* prefix is only 0.04 and is pruned. Bottom-left: even if t* enters the candidate set, generation probability ranks it 14th, outside the top K. The right half shows CAPE's two fixes. Right bars: gray is the backbone, hatched is fixing one stage, dark blue is fixing both; the black line is the upper bound of ranking-only. On both LastFM setups, fixing one stage barely moves the needle; both together reach 17.2.](figs/2610.29298/fig1_two_failures.png)

## 3. Diagnosis: where exactly is the long tail lost?

This experiment asks whether a tail target never enters the candidate set, or enters but is pushed down by ranking.

The trained model is held fixed. For each user three candidate sets are built and all are ranked by generation probability; the test target is checked for presence in the set and in the top 10. The three sets are: normal beam width 50; width raised to 75; width 50 plus 25 extra tail items—the 25 tail items with the highest co-occurrence with the user history that are not already in the original set. The co-occurrence algorithm is in Section 4.

Two models are used: MiniOneRec (generative recommendation on Qwen2.5-1.5B) on I&S, Office, and LastFM; TIGER (a classic encoder–decoder generative retriever) on LastFM, averaged over three random seeds.

| Data / model | Tail test users | Width 50: share of tail targets in candidates / top-10 hits | Width 75: share / top-10 | Extra 25: new tail targets in set / of which in top 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I&S / MiniOneRec | 2,622 | 11.94% / 96 | 14.45% / 95 | 135 / 0 |
| Office / MiniOneRec | 2,485 | 10.50% / 141 | 13.04% / 142 | 159 / 9 |
| LastFM / MiniOneRec | 634 | 8.04% / 50 | 9.31% / 55 | 98 / 6 |
| LastFM / TIGER | 634 | 5.21% / 25.0 | 5.63% / 25.0 | 107.3 / 0 |

Start with retrieval. At width 50 only 5.21%–11.94% of tail targets enter the candidate set; ==the remaining eight or nine tenths cannot be helped by any later ranking==. Widening by 50% brings in 66 and 63 more tail targets on I&S and Office, but top-10 hits change by −1 and +1; on LastFM at most 8 more enter. The extra 25 beams still cover the next-highest-probability prefixes, which are mostly head items.

Then ranking. The extra 25 tail items do bring many targets in—135 on I&S—but after generation-probability ranking, 0 of them enter the top 10. ==Generation probability itself favors head items, so even when a tail target enters the set it ranks behind head items==.

One more ratio will be used later: among tail targets missed at width 50, the share that rank in the user's top-50 tail items by co-occurrence with history is 8.2% on I&S, 9.6% on Office, and 24.0% / 25.5% on the two LastFM setups. Co-occurrence recovers clearly more on LastFM.

The authors attribute this to the memorization–generalization pair from Wide & Deep. Recommenders have two skills: remembering which two items co-occur (memorization) and generalizing to unseen combinations through shared representations. Generative models decide via shared prefixes and lean toward generalization; they lack item-pair memorization, which is exactly what item-based collaborative filtering provides.

## 4. Method: expand recall by one path, add one term to ranking

CAPE stands for Co-occurrence-Aware Pool Expansion. It changes no model parameters, no ID encoding, and no beam search; every change is added outside the model at inference. A request runs in three steps.

![One request. Top row is the backbone: read user history H_u and beam-search 50 candidates. Bottom row is what CAPE adds: look up two offline co-occurrence tables U and W, pick 25 tail items outside the 50 with the highest co-occurrence with history; have the backbone score those 25 once (the dashed teacher-forcing line); then rerank all 75 by generation probability plus co-occurrence, locking the first slot to the backbone's first item.](figs/2610.29298/fig2_cape_pipeline.png)

**Step 1: add a tail-candidate path.** Offline, build a table $U[j,c]$: how many users interacted with both item $j$ and item $c$. Online, sum the rows of that table for each item in the user history to get $S_u(c)=\sum_p U[i_p,c]$, then take the top 25 among items that are tail and not already in the original 50. Counting users rather than interactions keeps a few heavy users from deciding what is added.

CAPE leaves the backbone's rank-1 item untouched and only rescores positions 2 through 10. That makes the launch blast radius easy to explain: the head result matches the backbone exactly, and only the later slots change.

papers.title: PerSPL: Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning
papers.authors: Xiaoan Xu, Tingzhou Wei, Juncheng Dong, Korel Gundem, Ethan X. Fang, Zhengling Qi
papers.summary: Personalized reward models score replies per user, but each user labels only a few dozen preference pairs, so most unlabeled replies go unused. Pairwise loss only constrains the score gap under the same prompt, so ==scores from different prompts can shift as a whole and a single reply cannot be judged with one threshold==. PerSPL pushes each labeled pair's mean score toward 0 so scores are comparable across prompts, fits a monotonic score-to-preference map per user, and only pseudo-labels high-confidence unlabeled replies before iterative retraining. On PersonalLLM, unseen-user accuracy is 95.5% versus 94.0% for the strongest baseline LoRe.

deep_reading.title: PerSPL: Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning
deep_reading.content:
A personalized reward model has to give the same response different scores for different users, and its training data are user-labeled preference pairs: two responses to the same prompt, and which one the user chose. Such labels are expensive; each user has only a few dozen pairs, and a new user may have a dozen or so. Meanwhile the model can generate as many responses as you like, they just come with no user and no preference label. This paper from Duke University and George Washington University, PerSPL, turns that unlabeled pool into per-user training data. ==During training it first pushes the mean score of each labeled pair toward 0, so that scores from different prompts become comparable==. It then fits, for each user, a monotone "score → probability of being chosen" curve, pseudo-labels only the unlabeled responses it is confident about, and retrains repeatedly on those together with the labeled data. On four benchmarks, PersonalLLM, HelpSteer2, Reddit TLDR (Reddit post-summary preferences) and Chatbot Arena, PerSPL has the highest average accuracy for both seen and new users. Broken down, though, the gains land mainly on seen users. In the authors' own ablation, unlabeled data improve new users by only 0 to 0.6 points, within the error bars.

## 1. Why unlabeled responses can't be used directly

Reward models are usually trained with the Bradley–Terry (BT) loss: user $u$ prefers $y^+$ over $y^-$ for prompt $x$, and the model scores them $r^+$ and $r^-$,

$$L_{BT}=-\log\sigma(r^+-r^-)$$

This loss looks only at the difference between the two scores. Add 100 to both scores for the same prompt and the loss is unchanged, as is the ordering within that prompt.

That is fine for comparing two responses to the same prompt, but it becomes a problem for a single unlabeled response. To pseudo-label a response as "this user will like it" or "won't", you have to compare its score with a threshold shared across prompts. The paper's example: prompt a's two responses score (101, 100) and prompt b's score (1, 0). Both are ordered correctly within their prompt, but prompt b's chosen response (1) is lower than prompt a's rejected one (100), and no single threshold separates them. The authors call this score-coordinate ambiguity: the pairwise loss pins down the difference but not where each pair sits as a whole. Note that this only affects cross-prompt comparison and single-response classification. If you only pick the best of N responses to the same prompt, any offset added to the whole prompt cancels out.

Existing semi-supervised reward-model methods learn a single reward shared by all users and pseudo-label with one global threshold, so they cannot handle "the same response has different labels for different users".

![The PerSPL pipeline (paper Figure 1). Top left: a few labeled pairs per user (green dots chosen, red crosses rejected); bottom left: the shared unlabeled response pool. The three middle rows show each user's score distribution and threshold δ: the same unlabeled responses (triangles) are sorted into pseudo-chosen, pseudo-rejected or abstain (grey question marks) differently for each user. Bottom right: how the pseudo-label sets change over iterations.](figs/2610.29219/fig1_overview.png)

## 2. Method

### 2.1 Score centering

Since nothing constrains the mean of each pair's scores, add a term that pushes it toward 0:

$$L_{reg}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{r^++r^-}{2}\right)^2\right]$$

The expectation runs over all labeled pairs of all users. In the example above, both pairs get pulled to about (0.5, −0.5): the within-prompt ordering is unchanged and the cross-prompt comparison becomes correct. All main experiments use weight $\lambda_r=0.01$ for this term.

The appendix gives a theoretical analysis of this term. In a linear model under a Gaussian assumption, the authors prove that adding a small centering term raises single-response classification accuracy at first order in $\lambda$, while the pairwise loss worsens only at second order, so at small weights it is almost free. There is a precondition, though. The variance structure of what the pair "shares" must not be aligned with the direction of what "differs". Then the centering term rotates the scoring direction toward one better suited to single-response classification. If the two are aligned, it only rescales the scores and brings nothing. On real data, the authors swept $\lambda_r$ on HelpSteer2 and Reddit TLDR. At 0.01, same-prompt pairwise accuracy changes by −0.02±0.14 and 0.00±0.36 points, so pairwise judgments are indeed unharmed. Precision of the most confident 10% of candidate pseudo-labels rises by 2.16 points on HelpSteer2, while on Reddit the change has an interval containing 0.

### 2.2 One calibration curve per user

With comparable scores, the next step is to set each user's threshold. For each of user $u$'s labeled pairs, label the chosen response's score 1 and the rejected one's 0, and fit a monotone non-decreasing function $f_u$ by isotonic regression, giving "the probability that this score falls on the chosen side". The first point where $f_u$ reaches 0.5 is the user's threshold $\delta_u$.

For an unlabeled response, compute its score $r$ for user $u$. If $f_u(r)>\tau$ it is labeled liked, if $f_u(r)<1-\tau$ disliked, and anything in between is abstained on and left out of training. The pseudo-label loss uses $\delta_u$ as the boundary:

$$L_{unlabel}=-\mathbb{E}\left[z\log\sigma(r-\delta_u)+(1-z)\log\sigma(\delta_u-r)\right]$$

$z$ is the pseudo-label. The same response lands at different points on different users' curves, so it can receive different labels.

### 2.3 Iterative self-training

The first round trains only on labeled data plus the centering term, giving an initial model and each user's calibration curve. Each later round re-pseudo-labels the unlabeled pool with the current model (drawing 1,000 candidates from the pool per user each time), reinitializes the model, and trains on $\alpha L_{label}+(1-\alpha)L_{unlabel}+\lambda_r L_{reg}$. Calibration curves are fitted on labeled data only, so pseudo-label errors cannot feed back into the thresholds.

The architecture is the same as the LoRe baseline: on top of a frozen 4,096-dimensional last-token LM representation, it learns a set of low-rank linear bases plus, for each user, mixture weights on a simplex. A new user fits only their own mixture weights and the bases stay fixed. So PerSPL differs from LoRe only in training data and loss.

## 3. Experiments

The four benchmarks span two axes, "are the responses real" and "are the users real": PersonalLLM has synthetic responses and simulated users; HelpSteer2 has human-rated responses and users simulated from attribute weights; Reddit TLDR and Chatbot Arena have real preferences from real users. Seen users take part in joint training; new users adapt from a small support set only. The metric is within-prompt pairwise accuracy, averaged over five random seeds.

### 3.1 Main results

The seven baselines are user-agnostic BT, two methods that feed user information into the model, two methods that add a small per-user module (one of them LoRe), the meta-learning method MRM, and the off-the-shelf Skywork V2 reward model. The table lists the most representative:

| Method | PersonalLLM seen/new | HelpSteer2 seen/new | Reddit TLDR (100 pairs) seen/new | Chatbot Arena seen/new |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BT | 88.8 / 89.0 | 63.0 / 63.2 | 63.2 / 64.3 | 80.3 / 78.1 |
| LoRe | 94.6 / 94.0 | 69.6 / 70.1 | 65.3 / 68.4 | 81.3 / 78.4 |
| MRM | 91.6 / 92.0 | 70.7 / 70.9 | 70.0 / 69.8 | 80.7 / 77.2 |
| **PerSPL** | **95.7 / 95.5** | **71.6 / 71.2** | **70.7 / 70.1** | **83.0 / 81.0** |

PerSPL has the highest mean in every column. Against LoRe, which shares its architecture, seen-user accuracy on Reddit TLDR rises from 65.3 to 70.7. In paired bootstrap tests against the strongest baseline in each setting, every interval for seen users and overall excludes 0, and four of the five intervals for new users do.

Note that PerSPL uses different hyperparameters per benchmark. The confidence threshold $\tau$ ranges from 0.6 to 0.9, the learning rate from 0.01 to 0.3, the labeled-loss weight $\alpha$ from 0.6 to 0.8, and the basis rank is 2 or 5. The baselines each use one benchmark-level configuration, and the paper does not say on which data these configurations were chosen.

### 3.2 2×2 ablation: is it the centering term or the unlabeled data?

On two settings each of HelpSteer2 and Reddit TLDR, the centering term ($\lambda_r=0$) and unlabeled training (a single round) are switched on and off. The table shows two of the settings:

| Configuration | HelpSteer2 (0.1) seen / new | Reddit TLDR (150 pairs) seen / new |
|---|---|---|
| Full PerSPL | 71.6 / 71.2 | 70.9 / 70.3 |
| Unlabeled data, no centering | 66.5 / 69.7 | 62.5 / 62.5 |
| Centering, no unlabeled data | 70.9 / 71.0 | 69.1 / 70.3 |
| Neither | 70.9 / 71.1 | 69.0 / 69.6 |

Adding only the centering term changes seen-user accuracy by at most ±0.1. Adding unlabeled data without centering costs seen users 2.9 to 6.5 points across the four settings; adding it with centering gains 0.5 to 1.8. So the centering term barely helps on its own; ==its job is to turn unlabeled data from harmful into useful==.

The new-user column calls for a discount on that conclusion. With centering on, adding unlabeled data gains new users only 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0 points across the four settings, while the standard deviations of these results are 0.5 to 1.0. That is, PerSPL's lead on new users in the main table comes more from centering and the overall training configuration than from the unlabeled data itself. This fits the design: a new user fits only their own mixture weights, and unlabeled data mainly improve the bases learned on seen users.

![Both panels are the same model trained on labeled data only; the only difference is the centering weight (left 0, right 0.01). Green is the score distribution of chosen responses, red of rejected ones. On the left the two overlap heavily and sit between 5 and 25; on the right they separate around 0 with much less overlap, and only then does a single threshold make sense.](figs/2610.29219/fig2_centering.png)

### 3.3 Hyperparameter sensitivity

![One-at-a-time sensitivity on HelpSteer2 (paper Figure 6). Left to right: varying the confidence threshold τ, the learning rate η and the labeled-loss weight α; the star marks the main configuration.](figs/2610.29219/fig6_sensitivity.png)

Varying the confidence threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 moves overall accuracy by only 0.30 points. $\tau=0.5$, which means no abstention at all and pseudo-labeling every candidate, is only 0.19 points below the main configuration. Varying $\alpha$ from 0.4 to 0.9 spans 0.23 points. So "pseudo-label only confident responses" does very little here; what matters is that centering makes scores comparable and thresholds trustworthy. The learning rate matters more: going from 0.01 to 0.3 loses 2.75 points.

### 3.4 Label noise, label budget and distribution shift

Against the strongest baseline MRM on HelpSteer2, as the fraction of randomly flipped preference labels goes from 0 to 0.5, PerSPL stays ahead, and its lead grows with the noise. With half the labels flipped it leads by 6.69 points, suggesting calibration and pseudo-labels partly correct noisy labels. As seen users' labels grow from 50 to 200 pairs, PerSPL's lead stays around 1 point and does not vanish with more labels.

The distribution-shift experiment tests whether the unlabeled pool still helps when its responses come from other generators. On PersonalLLM with a fixed 20% label flip (to avoid saturated accuracy), the default responses come from six generators including GPT-4o and Claude 3. The share of the unlabeled pool drawn from two unseen generators, Command R+ and GPT-4 Turbo, varies from 0 to 1. Relative to a labeled-only model, the overall gain falls from 3.21 to 0.66 points, with every interval above 0. Broken down, when the pool is entirely from new generators, seen users are still 1.5 points higher, while new users score 82.45 against 82.66, slightly below not using unlabeled data at all. That matches the observation in Section 3.2.

## 4. Limitations

The authors list these in the appendix. Each user's calibration curve needs labels as anchors, so zero-shot new users are out of scope. Filtering pseudo-labels by confidence may overrepresent "easy" response regions, and the authors did not measure pseudo-label precision and coverage by user subgroup. Distribution shift is tested with only two generators. All experiments train a reward head on frozen representations, with no end-to-end fine-tuning control. There are at most 200 users, so behavior at production scale is unknown. Only English instruction following, dialogue and summarization are tested. In addition, the LoRe baseline's code is licensed for academic use only.

One more: the experiments evaluate the reward model's pairwise accuracy and never plug it into downstream policy training or response selection.

## 5. Practical implications

If you build personalized ranking or personalized reward models and have plenty of unlabeled candidates, PerSPL's first step is the one most worth borrowing. Add a term to the pairwise loss that pushes each pair's mean score toward 0, then check whether scores across different requests are comparable. The ablation shows this step is a prerequisite: without it, self-training loses 3 to 6 points. The second step, fitting per-user isotonic calibration and pseudo-labeling unlabeled responses, gives existing users 0.5 to 1.8 points. For new users, this paper's data are not enough to show it helps.

papers.authors: Zhanshuo Cao, Jiakai Tang, Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu
papers.summary: When a sequential recommender encodes each historical behavior, ==some behaviors converge after one layer while others need several stacked layers to stabilize==. In a three-layer SASRec, 76.1% of behaviors are stable after the first layer and 6.7% need the third. LoopRec lets each historical behavior choose how many layers to stack instead of sharing one depth for the whole request. On the Amazon Software dataset with a SASRec backbone, NDCG@20 rises 5.68% relatively.

deep_reading.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
deep_reading.content:
Sequential recommenders predict the next item from a user's time-ordered history; the usual approach stacks the same number of encoding layers for every historical behavior. Diagnosing a trained three-layer SASRec, the authors find 76.1% of behaviors already converge after one layer of representation, while 6.7% need all three layers to stabilize—and both kinds often sit in the same sequence. ==A uniform depth wastes compute on already-converged behaviors and still under-computes the few hard ones==. LoopRec lets each historical behavior choose how many layers to stack; depth is allocated per behavior, not per request. The core change is turning ==“how many layers” from a global hyperparameter into a property of each historical behavior==: hard behaviors can take more rounds, already-converged ones stop early.

The structure has three steps. First run the whole history through a shared encoding block—one Transformer block with reused parameters; then at each recursion boundary a gate (a light network that reads the current state and outputs an exit probability; the paper also calls it a router) decides per position whether to exit or continue, and only continuing positions run the same block again; finally read out the representation at each position's chosen depth and predict the next item. ==The only supervision is next-item cross-entropy==; training also adds two gate regularizers and a warmup. On three Amazon datasets and four backbone families, with a SASRec backbone on Amazon Software, NDCG@20 rises 5.68% relatively.

## 1. Motivation: why should every behavior pay the same depth

Almost every sequential encoder—attention, convolution, or linear recurrence—gives every historical behavior the same number of layers. Something casually opened three months ago and something repeatedly viewed yesterday cost the same compute.

Before proposing a method the authors run two diagnoses. The opening numbers come from the first: in SASRec (a classic self-attention sequential recommender), stop updating one position at a time and take the shallowest layer after which the recommendation set no longer changes as that position's saturation depth. Shallow- and deep-saturating positions mix in the same sequence, so ==no fixed depth covers all of them==.

![Mixture of shallow- and deep-saturating positions in one sequence; this diagnosis measures stability inside a fixed model.](figs/2610.30128/rethinking_truncation_jaccard_office_sasrec3l_top30_refstyle_preview.svg)

The second is more direct: only vary the depth of the latest five behaviors and let an offline searcher that sees the true target pick the best depth assignment. That searcher sees the answer and is only an analysis tool—the online router never sees the future target. It asks: if each behavior's depth can be chosen separately, can metrics beat a uniform depth? Yes—and the searcher's assignments ==often use less total compute==. These two diagnoses are more persuasive than the method itself because they show, before any new model, that per-behavior depth allocation has real headroom.

## 2. Method: one block reused, ask each round whether to continue

Why share parameters? If every layer had different parameters, positions that exit at layer 2 and layer 4 would live in different representation spaces and could not be scored together. LoopRec's answer is one encoding block, called repeatedly, so ==no matter which round a position exits, the representation comes from the same parameters==. The paper writes structures as LxRy: $x$ is layers in the shared block, $y$ is max recursions—e.g. L2R3 is a two-layer block used up to three times.

Shared-block recursion is a looped Transformer; Universal Transformer already combined shared recursion with per-position halting, and MoR (Mixture-of-Recursions) does token-level recursive depth on LMs. The decision style differs: MoR either assigns each token a total depth up front or picks a fixed-capacity top-k to continue each step; LoopRec re-judges every round from the current context with a binary stop/continue and needs no top-k. For recommendation, per-round binary decisions fit better than fixed capacity because user sequences vary a lot in length and information density, and a fixed top-k capacity is hard to set.

Concretely, an initial pass encodes the full history once. At each recursion boundary the gate reads each active position's current state and recursion index and outputs a scalar, turned by sigmoid into an exit probability:

$$p_i^{(r)}=\sigma(g(h_i^{(r)},e_r)).$$

$i$ is history position, $r$ current recursion depth, $h$ that position's state, $e$ a depth encoding, $g$ a light gate network, $\sigma$ sigmoid. Above a threshold the position stops; otherwise it continues. Judging after every position has absorbed one round of context is more reasonable than fixing depth up front, because each position's state already carries full-sequence information.

Only continuing positions form the next input, keeping relative order under a causal mask so each position sees only earlier behaviors. Stopped positions freeze their state. At max recursion, remaining positions are forced to stop.

Implementation has an easy-to-miss pitfall. The next round only processes continuing positions, so both length and content of the sequence change; active-position indices and order must be maintained carefully, or the same request yields different results across batches. How well dynamic position compression is done also decides whether speed gains materialize.

Readout combines each position's input vector with the state at its chosen depth. Forward uses hard depth; depth-related weights still backprop through routing probabilities, so the gate learns directly from the recommendation objective with no depth labels. The shared block keeps parameter count from growing with depth; depth-aware readout links the stop decision to the final prediction.

The biggest training hazard is routing collapse: if every position exits in the same round, the model degenerates to fixed depth. A depth-usage regularizer combines the hard-routing share with soft probability mass to keep depths from bunching.

Another regularizer stops the gate from emitting extreme scores too early. Once probabilities saturate early, stop choices freeze and immature early states lock the training trajectory. The authors borrow MoE's router z-loss to penalize a large log-partition of the binary gate.

The full objective:

$$L=L_{rec}+\lambda_b L_{bal}+\lambda_z L_z.$$

$L_{rec}$ is next-item cross-entropy, $L_{bal}$ the depth-usage regularizer, $L_z$ the gate stabilizer; $\lambda_b$ and $\lambda_z$ scale the two regularizers. The last two only constrain routing; item-prediction supervision is still only the target item.

There is also a warmup: during warmup every valid position runs to max depth with routing regularizers off, so the shared trunk learns usable states before the gate turns on. Ablating warmup drops all three datasets, most on Software, so it is not optional. The knobs to watch are shared-block depth, max recursions, and warmup length—they jointly decide whether training works and how large the compute budget is.

A walk-through of one request (illustration). The user recently saw A, B, C, D, E; the candidate is F. Initial encoding lets all five exchange context. The first gate exits A and B; C, D, E continue; next round C exits; D and E run to the budget. The model reads out at each chosen state and scores F. Exit trajectories and letters are examples; online the router never uses the true next item.

![Watch positions exit round by round along the shared encoding block; each gate only adds compute for continuing positions, then a unified readout.](figs/2610.30128/LoopRec_overview.svg)

## 3. Core contribution: how compute is allocated is part of modeling

Past sequential-model gains usually lengthen or deepen the whole sequence uniformly. This paper lets the model learn from data which behaviors need more stacked layers, and decides round by round from updated context—more flexible than assigning depth once.

Learned patterns also make sense. Newer behaviors and colder items are more often assigned deep layers. ==Cold items have weak statistics, so their representations need more stacked rounds to converge==; recent behaviors are closer to current intent, so spending more compute is reasonable. Heuristics by position or frequency underperform learned routing on average—so rules cannot simply replace learning.

A Seq-level Loop control shares recursion but loops the whole sequence together with no per-position exit. Pure shared recursion already captures part of the gain; per-position depth adds more on top, by how much depending on the dataset. ==This ablation separates the contributions of parameter reuse and compute allocation==—the experiment that matters most for interpreting the method.

Sharing the trunk also makes the method backbone-agnostic; the paper tests convolutional and linear-recurrent models too. They aggregate sequences differently but can all reuse an encoding block and let a gate decide which positions continue.

## 4. Results: quality and latency must be read separately

Experiments use Amazon Reviews 2023 Software, Office Products, and Patio. Each user's last interaction is the test; validation NDCG@20 selects models. NDCG is rank-discounted quality; MRR is the mean reciprocal rank of the true target. Main tables report five-run means.

NextItNet is a causal-convolution sequential model; LRURec is linear-recurrent; the four main backbones also include BSARec (SASRec plus a frequency-domain bias). Relative gains use the authors' reported values because absolute table metrics keep only four decimals.

Office Products gains are small. The fair reading: under matched fixed-depth controls, all four backbone families improve, with large amplitude differences.

Speed needs a clear scope. Tests are on one A6000 GPU for the encoder only, without full-candidate scoring. L2R4 versus a fixed model at the same max depth cuts encode time from 91.230 ms to 79.273 ms; L2R2 barely changes even when executed compute already fell.

Deeper structures leave more room for early exit; but ==dynamic branching, index maintenance, and many small matmuls eat part of the gain==. The authors acknowledge that only part of the skipped compute becomes wall-clock time. To judge online value, put encoding and candidate scoring into a full request together.

## 5. Limitations: speed gains depend on the runtime

Speed is only single-GPU encoder time; improvement amplitude varies a lot across recursive structures, and the authors state skipped compute only partly becomes wall-clock. They list sparsity-aware kernels and a learned max-recursion budget as future work; max recursion is still fixed before training.

Eval is on three same-source public datasets with hot-start history items. Industrial ultra-long behavior sequences, feature crosses, and candidate scoring have different cost structures that the paper does not cover.

If you have a user-sequence backbone, the cheapest first step is to log position, item frequency, and chosen depth beside it and check whether extra compute lands on recent or sparse behaviors.

Before shipping, compare speed against a fixed trunk at the same max effective depth—encoder latency and full-request latency separately. Add an ablation that keeps shared parameters but drops the adaptive gate to separate gains from parameter reuse versus compute allocation. For systems that personalize ranking from user history, these experiments map directly onto the quality–serving-cost trade-off. Longer sequences and deeper trunks are more worth trying, because more positions can exit early and more compute can be saved—provided the serving stack handles dynamic-length batches efficiently.

papers.title: RESEARCHHUB: A Personalized Literature Discovery System for Biomedical Preprints
papers.authors: Viswonathan Manoranjan, Taeyoon Kim, Nicholas Do, Sang Woo Kim, Dawei Li, Zhen Tan, Tianlong Chen, Yunmei Liu
papers.summary: ResearchHub recommends biomedical preprints over 44,937 MedRxiv papers from 2023–2025. Its core retriever PRISM is a dual-encoder: GPT-4o first writes researcher-style queries for each abstract, then ==contrastive loss plus cross-encoder distillation (MarginMSE) fine-tunes the encoder==. On those queries Recall@10 is 0.892, 12.4 points above SPECTER2-Search. Optional post-steps prefer results farther from the user's saved papers, DPP reranking to cut near-duplicates, and ordering from mainstream to specialized by local intrinsic dimension in embedding space.

papers.title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
papers.authors: Jian Zhong, Zeyu Liu, Pingchuan Cao, Rongduo Han, Shunye Tang, Guohuan Xie, Mingyuan Qin, Ran Ji, Xiao Liang, Wei Wang, Haining Zhang
papers.summary: Long-horizon assistants must remember user preferences and update them when preferences truly change. Common practice appends or overwrites by rule each turn, so ==one casual remark can overwrite an old memory==. PreCoMem stores a confidence on each memory and computes a surprise score each turn: how far the new content is from retrieved memories and whether they conflict; the score is lowered when retrieval is diffuse. Low scores reinforce existing memory, mid-range scores become low-confidence hypotheses, and only high, reliable scores down-weight old facts. On LongMemEval-S with gpt-4.1 answering, overall accuracy is 89.39% versus 86.16% for EverMemOS.

papers.title: SOAR: Social and Opinion-Aware Recommendations
papers.summary: SOAR recommends points of interest on Yelp by folding review sentiment and friend ties into the score: each place gets an initial score from public review polarity, then friends' reviews add or subtract. Versus a baseline without reviews or friends, Top-10 recall rises from 47.01% to 56.59% and Top-1 from 13.37% to 16.37%. Expanding friends to friends-of-friends barely changes quality while prediction speed falls from 55.56 to 7.32 requests per second. ==The paper compares only against this self-built baseline==.

papers.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
papers.authors: Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, Leshem Choshen
papers.summary: RAG stages—embedding models, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query rewrite, context compression, agentic checks—are usually evaluated alone. LASAGNA runs 450 configs on 8 benchmarks with corpora from 5K to 200K documents to measure how much single-component gains survive when combined. The three strongest retrieval techniques alone would sum to NDCG@10 +47%, but together only +17%; ==the components that raise retrieval are not the same ones that raise answer faithfulness==. A setup that leads on a small corpus trails by 13.7% NDCG@10 at 200K documents, with rank flips starting at 25K.

papers.title: From LOOP to Graph Exploration: Evolution of an AutoResearch System Architecture for Algorithm Models
papers.summary: Meituan moved Karpathy's AutoResearch (an agent edits training code, runs experiments, and keeps or rolls back by eval) onto its cloud training platform and rebuilt it three times in three months. V1 triggers a single agent with a cron script; V2 opens a new session each trigger, restores progress from a JSON state file, and ==no longer waits synchronously for training==; V3 has a lead agent split the problem into 3–4 mutually exclusive hypotheses explored by parallel branches and then merged. On two modeling projects, single-task time fell about 85% and 83% versus humans; one model shipped the system's proposals fully, and a multi-objective project beat the human baseline on all 12 prediction targets.

papers.title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
papers.authors: Dongfang Li, Zhuoen Chen, Bonian Jia, Zixuan Liu, Zhengxuan Lu
papers.summary: This is a framework paper with no new model and no experimental numbers. The authors argue that an agent's external memory should be judged by whether later actions improve, not only by whether old facts can be recalled. They classify memory along three axes: where state lives (context, external store, model parameters, …), what form it takes (episodic records, semantic knowledge, procedures), and which write/update policies apply. Evaluation should test retention under distraction, adaptation after environment change, and cross-task transfer, with "keep memory" versus "reset every time" controls so ==memory gains are separated from simply lengthening context==.
